title: Microsoft quietly retires the Copilot+ PC brand a little over two years in
subtitle: The 2026 Surface Pro and Laptop meet the Copilot+ hardware bar but ship without the label, and Qualcomm signals the badge is unlikely to return.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Microsoft is dropping the 'Copilot+ PC' name from its Windows-on-Arm and AI-accelerated laptop line, roughly two years after launching the category in mid-2024. Surface CVP Brett Ostrum confirmed that the newest Surface Pro and Surface Laptop 'are not called Copilot+ PCs' even though they clear the original Copilot+ hardware bar, and Qualcomm's SVP of compute and gaming has said the badge is unlikely to appear on future partner devices. The messaging is shifting toward 'AI on the edge' and hybrid on-device/cloud framing.

The retirement is a marketing decision, not a product one — the hardware requirements (a 40-plus TOPS NPU, minimum RAM and storage) are still enforced under the covers, and Windows continues to route features like Live Captions and Studio Effects through the NPU when it is present. What is going away is the badge that tied the platform to Recall, the on-device screenshot-and-search feature that shipped late, then shipped disabled after security researchers found it stored a searchable database of everything a user did in plaintext. Copilot+ launched with Recall as its lead demo and never fully recovered when Recall did not.

The broader read is that consumer AI-PC branding has struggled everywhere in 2025 and 2026. Apple has quietly renamed most of its 'Apple Intelligence' features to task-level names inside apps, Qualcomm's Snapdragon X marketing has moved toward performance-per-watt benchmarks rather than AI framing, and PC OEMs at IFA 2026 leaned harder on gaming and thin-and-light angles than on on-device AI. Enterprise buying, where AI-PC narratives were supposed to drive a refresh cycle, has instead concentrated on Microsoft 365 Copilot licensing rather than the physical hardware.

For learners: this is a useful case study in the difference between a category and a brand. The category — laptops with a real neural accelerator that can run a small model locally — is genuinely useful and still growing. The brand — 'Copilot+ PC' — died because it was pinned to a single flagship feature that failed to ship as promised. If you are ever tempted to build a product name around one unproven feature, look at what happened here and pick a name that describes what the hardware is, not the demo you hope will land.
